title: Distribution, Supply Chain and Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett

web_blocks.text: TARIL is principally a direct-to-customer, engineered-equipment supplier. The buyer is typically a utility, generator, EPC contractor or industrial customer that defines a technical specification and evaluates vendors for design, qualification, price, delivery and service. Orders arise through tendering and negotiated project processes; the company’s FY26 disclosures say it selected orders partly for margin profile, payment terms and alignment with production capacity. The public materials do not describe a dealer-led route, so the most defensible description is direct institutional selling with project-specific customer and EPC interfaces. [1][6]

The manufacturing footprint is concentrated in Gujarat at Changodar, Moraiya and Odhav. TARIL reports combined installed capacity near 75,000 MVA by FY26, with expansion at Changodar and Moraiya and backward-integration projects for conductors, pressboard, bushings, fabrication, CRGO processing and radiators. The plan is to reduce supplier dependence, but it introduces commissioning and utilization risk: in October 2026 the company announced three Chiyada greenfield projects with commercial operations targeted from Q1 FY28, and a ₹1,250 crore investment plan. This is a large commitment relative to the recent operating base and should be assessed against milestones and cash generation. [1][16]

A transformer order is not a simple “ship today, collect today” transaction. The customer’s specification, design approval, procurement of copper, CRGO steel, insulation and bushings, production, factory acceptance tests, dispatch, site installation and final acceptance can span many months. In FY26, consolidated debtor days rose to 129 from 85, inventory days to 133 from 118, while payable days dropped to 62 from 109; the cash-conversion cycle widened to about 199 days. That shows why an order book can coexist with weak operating cash flow: materials and labor are paid before final customer cash is collected. [1][17]

Input exposure is substantial. Raw materials consumed were roughly 70% of FY26 consolidated revenue before considering inventory movements and purchases of traded items. Copper, grain-oriented electrical steel, insulation, bushings and fabricated components are important inputs; availability, specifications and supplier qualification can shape both delivery time and gross margin. Customer contracts may contain escalation or adjustment mechanisms, but the public materials do not provide a complete summary of their prevalence or effectiveness. It is therefore not safe to assume full pass-through when commodity costs move. The expanding integration program may improve control over selected components, while increasing fixed costs and commissioning demands. [1][17]

The billing pattern can partially reduce funding strain. Large engineered contracts often use staged payments tied to advance, manufacturing progress, dispatch or acceptance, but TARIL has not published a universal payment schedule that applies across orders. The FY26 cash-flow statement shows the net result of all contract terms: ₹280 crore cash use from trade receivables, ₹175 crore use from inventories, and ₹109 crore cash use from trade payables, partly offset by higher other liabilities. The company’s supplier-finance arrangement may support suppliers who choose to discount accepted bills, but it does not remove the need to monitor actual bank borrowings and payment obligations. [1][17]

web_blocks.caption: FY26 audited consolidated ₹100 revenue-to-cash waterfall; P&L values use the same FY and consolidated basis. Capex is cash purchases of PPE/CWIP/intangibles; FCF is CFO less capex.
web_blocks.takeaway: For each ₹100 of revenue, the group generated approximately ₹15.3 of operating EBITDA before interest and tax, but absorbed about ₹4.2 of cash in operating activities; after approximately ₹4.4 of cash capex, free cash flow was negative about ₹8.6. The key economic leak was working capital, not reported operating profit. [17][18]

web_blocks.text: The arithmetic behind the block is based on the audited FY26 consolidated statement. Revenue from operations was ₹2,508.80 crore; materials consumed plus inventory movement and stock purchases net to cost of goods around ₹1,694.87 crore; employees cost ₹105.74 crore; other operating expenses were ₹325.01 crore; depreciation ₹29.91 crore; finance cost ₹51.08 crore; other income ₹60.85 crore; tax ₹90.87 crore. Operating cash flow was negative ₹105.38 crore and investing cash flow was a modest outflow, including cash capital expenditure of ₹109.44 crore. The ₹100 model is illustrative: it scales audited annual figures, it does not claim every rupee of indirect costs is caused by one order. [17][18]

The cash-flow warning is not abstract. The FY26 audited report says higher receivables and inventory absorbed cash; the fundamentals snapshot records CFO of negative ₹105 crore against PAT of ₹272 crore. Borrowings rose as the business funded this timing gap. Management’s order selectivity and collection focus are rational responses, but the proof will be a shorter cash-conversion cycle and positive CFO through a full expansion cycle, not a statement that the backlog is “visible.” [1][17]

Working capital turns over only after each unit is accepted. TARIL pays for materials, labor, testing and dispatch before it receives final customer cash. Long lead times can stretch this interval. A larger order book therefore increases funding needs until collections catch up. The operating test is whether the company shortens debtor and inventory days while keeping supplier terms stable. Profit growth without that progress can still require new borrowing.

book_paragraphs: Let us follow one large order from the buyer’s desk to the bank account. First, an engineer translates a grid requirement into a specification. TARIL must pass vendor approval and technical evaluation. After a contract is awarded, it may need to place orders for long-lead inputs before most of the sale can be recognized. The factory then designs, winds, assembles, dries, tests and documents the unit. The customer inspects it before dispatch; the unit may travel by road or sea; site installation and acceptance can unlock the final payment. You can see the timing mismatch: cash leaves early and comes back in installments.

This is why order quality includes payment terms, not just the headline contract amount. The company has said it would avoid booking work too far beyond its delivery window and would be selective on margin and cash terms. That discipline can protect the factory from being overbooked. It can also reduce near-term order inflows if management walks away from low-quality work. Our scorecard should therefore pair backlog with order conversion, gross margin, customer advances, receivable days and operating cash flow.

The FY26 waterfall gives us a crisp picture. On each ₹100 of sales, materials and operating costs leave around ₹15 before depreciation and finance expense. Yet operating cash flow is negative because the balance sheet must carry work in progress, finished goods and unpaid customer invoices. A growing factory can worsen that gap before it improves it. The question is whether higher utilization and backward integration eventually lower cost and lead time enough to offset the working capital that long contracts demand.

TARIL’s expansion is partly about control. Making radiators or processing materials internally may reduce supplier delays and improve quality oversight. But “backward integration” is not automatically a margin gift. New plants need commissioning, trained operators, customer approval, maintenance and working capital of their own. A facility that stands idle can convert a supplier bill into depreciation without delivering a cost advantage. We should watch milestones and cash contribution by facility as closely as capacity announcements.

For this kind of manufacturer, raw materials are not a footnote. The core and windings are built from costly, specification-bound materials, and a late delivery can idle labor and capacity. If copper or electrical steel prices move between quotation and purchase, margin depends on contract clauses, the timing of procurement and the company’s ability to manage the exposure. Backward integration can provide more control over quality and delivery, but it does not eliminate exposure to upstream commodities. We should ask whether integration makes the factory faster and more reliable, not simply whether it adds more steps under one roof.

The audited cash-flow bridge makes working capital tangible. Trade receivables consumed about ₹280 crore of cash and inventory about ₹175 crore in FY26; trade payables consumed another ₹109 crore as the company paid suppliers faster. Other liabilities provided an offset, but not enough to prevent negative operating cash flow. That is the cost of project growth on the balance sheet. The follow-up question is whether billing milestones and collections improve as work is delivered, or whether the larger plant needs a still larger pool of financing to carry the same business model.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: In project manufacturing, the order book is a promise of future work; the cash conversion cycle tells you how much of your own balance sheet must stand behind that promise.
